title: Building: menus and input
specPoints: 2.2.1 Programming fundamentals: **iteration** (condition-controlled loops), **selection**, **casting** between data types
2.3.1 Defensive design: **input validation** (range check, type check, presence check), **anticipating misuse**
Practical programming skills (Section B): write robust programs that reject invalid input and keep running
learn: Write a `get_int(prompt, low, high)` helper that performs type and range checks and only returns a valid integer
Write `get_text` (presence check) and `get_choice` (must be one of a set of options) helpers
Build a menu function that returns a validated choice, and a main loop that uses it
Reuse the helpers everywhere input is taken instead of repeating validation code
Test input code with erroneous data: blank, letters, decimals, negatives, out of range
hook: Type the word 'seven' into most students' programs where a number is expected and they crash with a red traceback. In Section B, 'the program must reject invalid input' is a mark — and in a real program it is the difference between software and a toy. Today you write three small helpers once, and never write validation code again.

video.title: Three helpers you will use forever
video.brief: 4 minutes. A program asks 'Year group:' and the user types 'ten' — crash. Rewind. The same prompt now goes through `get_int('Year group: ', 7, 11)`: 'ten' is rejected, '12' is rejected, '9' is accepted. Zoom into the helper: `while True`, `isdigit`, range compare, `return`. Then `get_text` for blanks and `get_choice` for y/n. Finally the menu becomes `get_int('Choice: ', 1, 6)` — one line — and the main loop is six lines long. End with a test table of erroneous inputs, all handled.

p: A menu program takes input in five or six places. If each place has its own validation, that is five or six copies of the same loop — and five or six places for a bug. Instead write **one helper function** per kind of input and call it everywhere. `get_int` handles whole numbers in a range; `get_text` handles text that must not be blank; `get_choice` handles 'one of these options'. Each one **loops until the input is valid** and then **returns** it, so the calling code never sees bad data.

explain.h: get_int: type check then range check
p: The order matters. `isdigit()` is the **type check** — it is true only for strings made of digits 0–9, so `""`, `"ten"`, `"-3"` and `"2.5"` all fail it. Only after that is it safe to call `int()` and do the **range check**. `while True` with a `return` inside is the standard pattern: the loop can only be left by returning a valid value.

`get_text` is a **presence check**: `strip()` removes spaces so `"   "` counts as blank. `get_choice` takes a list of allowed answers and lowercases the input so `Y` and `y` both work — that is a **format check** plus a lookup. The menu is then just `get_int("Choice: ", 1, 6)`: the type and range checks do all the work, and the main loop can trust that `choice` is 1 to 6.

Input helpers are tested with **erroneous and boundary data**, not normal data — normal data would work without the helper. For `get_int(prompt, 7, 11)` the test set is: 6 and 12 (just outside), 7 and 11 (boundaries, accepted), blank, a word, a decimal, a negative, a number with a space. Write the expected message for each **before** you run. In a Section B refine question, 'add validation so that…' is answered by exactly the loop in `get_int`.
Write the checking code once in a function. Call the function every time you need input. Less code, fewer bugs.

list: Is it all digits? If not, say so and ask again.
Is it in range? If not, say so and ask again.
If both pass, `return int(text)`. That ends the loop.

p: Try blank, a word, a decimal, a negative, too small, too big. The program must say something sensible and ask again, never crash.

keyterms.def: Checking that input is sensible and in the expected form before the program uses it.
Checking that input is the right kind of data, e.g. all digits before converting to an integer.
Checking that a number is between an allowed minimum and maximum.
Checking that something has been entered and the input is not blank.
A small reusable function that does one job, such as getting a valid integer, for the rest of the program.
Input of the wrong type or form that the program should reject without crashing.

try.title: 1. Break get_int, then confirm it holds
p: Run this with each of these inputs in turn, typing the next one when asked again: `ten`, blank, `2.5`, `-3`, `6`, `12`, then `9`. Write down the message you got for each. Then **remove** the `isdigit` check and run again with `ten` to see why the type check must come first.

try.title: 2. Write get_text and get_choice
p: Complete the two helpers so that the tests at the bottom behave as the comments say. `get_text` must reject blank and spaces-only input. `get_choice` must accept any case and reject anything not in the options list.
try.code:
def get_text(prompt):
    """Keep asking until the input is not blank."""
    pass

def get_choice(prompt, options):
    """Keep asking until the input (lowercased) is one of the options."""
    pass

# tests: type a blank line, then three spaces, then Ada - expect two 'cannot be blank' messages
name = get_text("Name: ")
print("Got:", name)
# tests: type maybe, then Y - expect one error message then y
answer = get_choice("Save? (y/n): ", ["y", "n"])
print("Got:", answer)

try.title: 3. The validated menu and main loop
p: Put the three helpers together with the club register. Complete `show_menu()` so it prints the options and returns a validated integer 1–6. Then make `add_member` use `get_text` for the name and `get_int` for the year (7–11), and `award_points` use `get_int` for the points (1–100). Test with: menu choice `9`, `x`, blank, then `2`; name blank then `Tim`; year `12` then `8`; then `1`; then `6`.

try.title: 4. Refine: a confirmation and a float helper
p: Two refinements from a changed brief. (a) `remove_member` must ask 'Are you sure? (y/n)' using `get_choice` and only remove on `y`. (b) The club now records subs paid as money, so write `get_float(prompt, low, high)` that accepts `2.50` and `3` but rejects `abc`, blank and `-1`. Hint: `try: value = float(text) except ValueError:` is one way; another is to check the text has at most one `.` and digits either side. Test both helpers with erroneous data.

try.title: 5. Save v2 with the helpers at the top
instructions: Save Try 3 (with your Try 4 refinements) as `club_v2.py`. Put the three helpers at the top of the file under a comment `# ---- input helpers ----` so you can copy that block into every future program, including the mini projects.

check.fb: The minus sign is not a digit, so negatives fail the type check.

check.q: In `get_int`, the type check must come before the range check because:
opts: `int()` on a word crashes, so we must know it is digits first
check.fb: Convert only after you know conversion is safe.

check.q: A presence check makes sure that:
opts: The input is in lower case

check.q: The best way to validate the menu choice is:
check.fb: Reuse the helper: type and range check in one call.

check.q: The most useful test data for an input helper is:
check.fb: The helper exists to handle bad input, so test it with bad input.

exam.q: A program asks the user to enter the number of tickets they want, from 1 to 8. Write a function `getTickets()` that keeps asking until a valid whole number is entered and then returns it.
model: Function header and a loop that continues until the input is valid (1). Input taken and checked to be a whole number / digits only (1). Range check 1 to 8 inclusive with a message if outside (1). Valid value returned as an integer (1).
exam.commentary: A write question. The loop must be able to repeat — a single `if` that prints an error and carries on scores the check but not the loop mark. `>= 1 and <= 8` or `> 0 and < 9` both fine; `> 1` loses the range mark because 1 is valid.

exam.q: The following code is intended to make sure the answer is y or n. Identify the error and rewrite the line so that `Y` and `N` are also accepted.
exam.code:
01 answer = input("Continue? (y/n): ")
02 while answer != "y" and answer != "n"
03     answer = input("Continue? (y/n): ")
04 endwhile
model: Capital letters are rejected / the comparison is case-sensitive (1). `answer = input(...).lower()` on lines 01 and 03, or `while answer.lower() != "y" and answer.lower() != "n"` on line 02 (1).
exam.commentary: Refine question: identify, then the changed line in code. Writing 'use lower case' in English scores the first mark only.

exam.q: A student says: 'My program validates the menu choice, so it does not need to validate the year group — the user has already shown they can type numbers.' Explain why the student is wrong.
model: Each input is separate / a user can type a valid choice and then an invalid year (1); without a check an invalid year (e.g. 15 or 'ten') would be stored or crash the program (1).
exam.commentary: Explain: the claim is wrong because… plus the consequence.

home: Add `get_float` and the confirmation to `club_v2.py`. Then write a ten-row test table for your three helpers: input, which check it should fail, expected message. Run every row and tick it.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 3 · explain 12 · try 33 · check 4 · exam 5 · homework 3
misconceptions: Validating with a single `if` so bad input is reported but the program carries on with it.
Calling `int(input())` and then checking — the crash happens before the check.
Thinking `isdigit()` accepts negative numbers or decimals.
Copying the validation loop into every function instead of calling the helper.
say: 'Can it crash? Then it is not validated.'
'Where is the return? Inside the loop, only on the good path.'
'You wrote that loop twice. Make it a function.'
teacher.skip: Try 4 (b) `get_float` can be homework. Try 1 → Try 3 is the build.
differentiation: Support: give `get_text` complete; students write `get_choice` by copying the pattern.
Stretch: make `get_int` accept an optional default so that pressing Enter returns it (e.g. year defaults to 7), and test the new boundary.
